content: Nafcillin sodium is an antibiotic approved by the FDA for treating staphylococcal infections. It is specifically indicated for infections caused by penicillinase-producing staphylococci that are susceptible to the drug. Initial culture and susceptibility tests should be performed to identify the causative organism and its sensitivity to nafcillin. In cases of suspected resistant staphylococcal infections, nafcillin may be used empirically before test results are available. However, it should not be used for infections caused by organisms susceptible to penicillin G. Therapy should be discontinued if susceptibility tests indicate the infection is due to an organism other than resistant Staphylococcus. To minimize the development of drug-resistant bacteria and maintain the effectiveness of nafcillin and other antibacterial drugs, it should only be used to treat or prevent infections proven or strongly suspected to be caused by susceptible bacteria. When culture and susceptibility data are available, they should guide the selection or modification of therapy. In the absence of such data, local epidemiology and susceptibility patterns may inform empiric therapy. Nafcillin is administered as an intravenous infusion. The standard adult dosage is 500 mg every 4 hours, with 1 g every 4 hours recommended for severe infections. The infusion should be administered slowly over 30 to 60 minutes to reduce the risk of vein irritation and extravasation. Bacteriologic studies should always be conducted to identify the causative organisms and their susceptibility to nafcillin. The duration of therapy depends on the type and severity of the infection and the patient’s overall condition, as determined by clinical and bacteriological response. For severe staphylococcal infections, therapy should continue for at least 14 days and for at least 48 hours after the patient becomes afebrile, asymptomatic, and cultures are negative. Endocarditis and osteomyelitis may require longer treatment durations. Nafcillin-probenecid therapy is generally reserved for infections requiring very high serum levels of nafcillin. No dosage adjustments are necessary for patients with renal dysfunction, including those on hemodialysis, as hemodialysis does not accelerate nafcillin clearance. However, in patients with hepatic insufficiency and renal failure, nafcillin serum levels should be monitored, and the dosage adjusted accordingly. In pediatric patients, nafcillin is used for bacterial meningitis caused by methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus and infective endocarditis caused by oxacillin-susceptible staphylococci. Dosages vary by age and weight. For neonates, the dosage is 75 mg/kg/day divided every 8 to 12 hours for those aged birth to 7 days, and 100 to 150 mg/kg/day divided every 6 to 8 hours for those aged 8 to 28 days. For children older than 28 days, the dosage is 200 mg/kg/day divided every 6 hours. For infective endocarditis, the dosage is 200 mg/kg/day (maximum dose: 12 g/day) divided into 4 to 6 doses, with or without gentamicin sulfate for native valve infections, and with rifampin and gentamicin sulfate for prosthetic valve infections. Safety and effectiveness in pediatric patients have not been established, and serum levels should be monitored due to immature hepatic and renal function. Nafcillin is contraindicated in patients with a history of hypersensitivity (anaphylactic) reactions to penicillins. Solutions containing dextrose may be contraindicated in patients with known corn allergies. Serious and occasionally fatal hypersensitivity reactions, including anaphylaxis, have been reported in patients receiving penicillin therapy. These reactions are more likely in individuals with a history of penicillin hypersensitivity or sensitivity to multiple allergens. Cross-reactivity with cephalosporins has been reported. If an allergic reaction occurs, nafcillin should be discontinued, and appropriate therapy initiated. Serious anaphylactic reactions require immediate emergency treatment with epinephrine, oxygen, intravenous steroids, and airway management as needed. Clostridium difficile-associated diarrhea (CDAD) has been reported with nearly all antibacterial agents, including nafcillin, and may range from mild diarrhea to fatal colitis. CDAD should be considered in all patients presenting with diarrhea following antibiotic use. If CDAD is suspected or confirmed, ongoing antibiotic use not directed against C. difficile may need to be discontinued, and appropriate management, including fluid and electrolyte replacement, protein supplementation, antibiotic treatment of C. difficile, and surgical evaluation, should be instituted as clinically indicated. Nafcillin is primarily cleared through the liver/biliary tract. Caution should be exercised when treating patients with concomitant hepatic insufficiency and renal dysfunction. Serum levels should be monitored, and the dosage adjusted to avoid potential neurotoxic reactions associated with very high concentrations. Prescribing nafcillin in the absence of a proven or strongly suspected bacterial infection or prophylactic indication increases the risk of developing drug-resistant bacteria. Adverse reactions to nafcillin include pain, swelling, inflammation, phlebitis, thrombophlebitis, pseudomembranous colitis, urticaria, and pruritus. Neurotoxic reactions, renal tubular damage, interstitial nephritis, and gastrointestinal irritation have also been reported. Local reactions such as severe tissue necrosis and skin sloughing may occur with intravenous administration. Agranulocytosis, neutropenia, and bone marrow depression have been associated with nafcillin use. Nafcillin may interact with other drugs. Tetracycline, a bacteriostatic antibiotic, may antagonize the bactericidal effect of penicillin, and concurrent use should be avoided. Nafcillin has been reported to decrease the effects of warfarin, necessitating close monitoring of prothrombin time and dose adjustment. When used with cyclosporine, nafcillin may result in subtherapeutic cyclosporine levels, requiring monitoring in organ transplant patients. Nafcillin is classified as Pregnancy Category B by the FDA. Animal reproduction studies have shown no evidence of harm to the fetus, but there are no adequate or well-controlled studies in pregnant women. It should be used during pregnancy only if clearly needed. Penicillins are excreted in human milk, and caution should be exercised when administered to nursing women. Nafcillin is supplied as a premixed frozen solution in single-dose Galaxy containers for intravenous use. It should be stored at or below -20°C (-4°F) and thawed before use. The thawed solution is stable for 21 days under refrigeration or 72 hours at room temperature. It should not be refrozen.
